t.shilin karst suogeyi village@24.7,103.3:
Shilin means Stone Forest, and the name is accurate: for several square kilometres on the Yunnan plateau, grey limestone pillars as tall as ten-storey buildings stand in clusters, like petrified trees. The rock was laid down in a shallow sea more than two hundred and fifty million years ago, then lifted, dissolved by rain and groundwater, and carved into needles, towers and narrow corridors. It forms part of the South China Karst, a UNESCO World Heritage listing that includes some of the world's most spectacular limestone scenery. Shilin lies about eighty kilometres from Kunming, at an altitude of roughly 1,700 metres, so the air is mild and spring-like for much of the year.

Suogeyi village is the human side of the picture. It belongs to the Sani, a branch of the Yi people, who have lived in this country for centuries and whose women wear embroidered headdresses in blue and pink. The village lies inside a quieter and less crowded area of the forest, with stone paths winding through the pillars and houses built of the same grey rock. The Sani are known for their folk epic, the story of Ashima, a girl who is carried off and turned into an echo in the stone, and some of the rock formations are named after her. The Torch Festival, in the summer, is the big annual gathering, with wrestling, dancing and fires.

The riding on the Yunnan plateau is worth the trip, though getting a bike there is another matter, since foreign riders in China normally need local registration, a Chinese licence and often a guide. If you do manage it, the roads around Shilin are good, with gentle curves, red soil fields, and lines of eucalyptus trees. Heavy trucks and buses are the main hazard, and rain can come in sudden downpours in summer. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with dry, clear days, and the tourist crowds are thinnest in the early morning.

Shilin town has fuel, hotels and restaurants, and is only about eleven kilometres away. Try rice noodles in a local shop, and the grilled goat cheese sold on sticks, a Yunnan speciality. If the main paths are packed, look for the quieter side trails, and bring a rain jacket.
t.chengjiang fossil site@24.7,103.0:
About 518 million years ago, in a shallow sea where Yunnan now stands on a high plateau, a sudden mud slide buried a community of soft-bodied animals so quickly that their outlines survived as fossils. Those fossils, found in the Maotianshan Shale near Chengjiang, are among the most important ever found, because they capture the Cambrian explosion, the rapid appearance of most major animal groups. They include early arthropods, worms with spiny legs and some of the oldest known relatives of vertebrates, preserved with details like eyes, guts and gills. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a small museum and viewing area explain what scientists have found.

The place is a hill of ordinary-looking grey and yellow rock, and it takes some imagination to see its meaning. Visitors usually get a good look at the exposed rock layers and the displays, with specimens that look like tiny, delicate drawings pressed into stone. It is a good reminder that deep time is real, and that the plateau you are standing on was once beneath the sea.

The surroundings are lovely. Chengjiang sits beside Fuxian Lake, one of the deepest freshwater lakes in China, with clear water and green hills around it, and the county is roughly an hour from Kunming, the provincial capital, known as the City of Eternal Spring for its mild climate. The roads here are mostly good, with expressways between the cities and winding local roads between hills, farmland and villages. Yunnan's elevation, well over a kilometre and a half, means that days are mild and nights cool, and the best seasons are spring and autumn, though rain falls mostly in summer.

Be realistic about the logistics. Motorcycle use by foreign visitors in China is tightly regulated, so check licence and permit requirements long before arrival. For fuel, services and food, use the larger towns along the main roads, as the nearest listed town in the data, Shilin, is about 40 km away. Yunnan is known for its food, from rice noodles served in a bowl of hot broth, which locals call crossing-the-bridge noodles, to wild mushrooms in season. A bowl of those noodles after the fossils makes a very good day.
t.ensemble mixte de fatu uku@-9.4,-138.9:
Fatu Uku, more often written Fatu Huku, is a lump of rock that most travellers only see from a boat. It lies in the Marquesas off the northeast tip of Hiva Oa, a bare, steep islet with cliffs plunging into deep water and a natural arch worn through its base. Nobody lives there. The only residents are seabirds, which nest on the ledges in noisy colonies, and the occasional goat that has somehow arrived.

Because of its isolation, it is a natural refuge, and the sea around it is part of a protected marine area. Fish are plentiful, manta rays glide through the channels, and divers say that the water has the sort of clarity that makes them forget depth. Sailors passing between Hiva Oa and the other islands give the islet a wide berth because the swells and currents between the rocks are unpredictable, and so rough days can cut off visits altogether.

Hiva Oa itself is worth the trip. Atuona, the main town, is where Paul Gauguin spent his last years and where the Belgian singer Jacques Brel also settled, and both are buried in the hillside cemetery above the bay, with the sea beyond. On the far side of the island, at Puamau, huge stone tiki stand in the forest, some of the largest in French Polynesia. Roads on Hiva Oa climb in tight switchbacks over ridges and plunge into valleys, and the landscape swings from dry cactus slopes to wet fern forest.

Fuel and food are limited and found in Atuona, so plan carefully, and ask locally about boats to the coast. Tours go out in small fishing boats when the weather allows. The calmer months from May to October make for the easiest crossings, and a light rain jacket never hurts. Pack patience as well, because everything works at island pace.
t.ipoh@4.6,101.1:
Ipoh is Malaysia's quiet third city, a place that was once rich from tin and now lives on its food. Around the Kinta valley, limestone hills rise abruptly from the flat plain like islands, their sides streaked and their caves home to Buddhist temples. Ipoh sits among them, with a colonial old town of shophouses, a grand railway station sometimes called the Taj Mahal of Ipoh, and a famous coffee culture. The white coffee here is roasted with margarine and served with condensed milk, and it is a point of local pride. The city has about 670,000 people, which gives it all the fuel and services you need.

The wealth that built the old town came from tin. In the nineteenth century, Chinese and Malay miners, and British investors, turned the Kinta valley into one of the richest tin-producing areas in the world, and the mansions and clan houses of that era remain. Walk through the Concubine Lane and the street art in the old town, and you can see the effect. Food is the main attraction: chicken with bean sprouts, hor fun noodles in broth, dim sum and egg tarts, plus pomelo, which grows in the district.

As a starting point for Cameron Highlands, Ipoh is easy. The road leaves the city through the suburbs and heads toward the hills, with the highway to Tapah and the turn-off onto the mountain road. Traffic is heavy in the city, and motorbikes are everywhere, so keep an eye on mirrors. The air is hot and humid, with afternoon storms common, so early starts are better. Fill the tank and eat well, because the climb ahead takes time.

Cave temples are a particular feature. Sam Poh Tong and Kek Lok Tong are carved into the limestone, with gardens and pools, and they make a cool stop. The best months are the drier period from December to March, though the weather in Malaysia is rarely predictable. The evenings are lively, with night markets, and the city is relaxed. It is the kind of place where the best plan is to eat twice and leave late.
t.ringlet@4.4,101.4:
Ringlet is a small farming town in the Cameron Highlands, in the cool uplands of Pahang, and it is the first place you reach after the long climb up from the lowlands. The road from Tapah is a famous one: it winds for more than fifty kilometres through tropical forest, with bends that tighten and slow, a vertical green wall on one side, and a steep drop on the other. The temperature falls steadily and the air gets thin and damp, so by the time you reach Ringlet, you have gone from steaming heat to something close to an English spring. A lake lies nearby, held back by a dam for hydropower in the 1960s, and its edges are lined with flower farms.

The highlands are named for William Cameron, a British surveyor who recorded the plateau in the 1880s, and the British quickly saw its value as a hill retreat from the heat. Tea, vegetables and flowers arrived, and that is what you see now: terraced farms, plastic greenhouses glowing white, and neat green rows of tea on the higher slopes. Ringlet is a working agricultural town more than a tourist one, and that is part of its appeal. Early in the morning, the market is a busy place, and the smell of fresh produce and wet soil is strong.

As a ride, the climb is a joy for those who enjoy a long, flowing, curving road, and a trial for those who do not like trucks. Lorries loaded with vegetables grind down the road, and tour buses wait for no one, so choose your moment and your overtakes. Mist and rain can be sudden, especially after midday, and the surface can be greasy. Drivers can be impatient. Leave early, and keep good distance.

For fuel, Tanah Rata, about six kilometres on, is a certain bet, and Brinchang has more stations still; Ringlet itself offers small shops and cafés for a drink and a snack. There are plenty of simple places for noodles, roti and tea. The temperatures in the evening can fall below what many riders expect, so pack a jacket, gloves and something warm for the night.
t.tanah rata@4.5,101.4:
Tanah Rata is the main town of the Cameron Highlands, a long street of shops, guesthouses, cafés and travel agents laid out along a valley at about 1,400 metres, and it hums with backpackers, tour groups and weekending families from Kuala Lumpur. The weather is the first thing that surprises people. It is cool, often cloudy, and on many evenings you will see locals in jackets and woolly hats. A few buildings in the Tudor style recall the colonial days, when the British came up here to escape the lowland heat, and the 1930s hotel on the slope still serves a very English afternoon tea.

What the highlands are famous for is tea, and the green slopes of the plantations around Tanah Rata are the signature view. The terraced bushes roll over the hills in a blanket of green, and a few estates, including the well-known BOH plantation founded in the 1920s, have tea rooms with views over the valley where you can sit with a pot and a scone. Strawberry farms and butterfly gardens round out the tourist circuit, and on Gunung Brinchang, the peak nearby, there is a mossy forest of twisted trees and ferns that feels more like a fairy tale than a tropical jungle.

As a place to ride through, Tanah Rata is slow. The traffic can be heavy at weekends, with buses and cars crawling along, and the roads out are narrow, winding and busy with scooters. The reward is the upper roads to the tea estates and the mossy forest, where bends are tight, the air is cool, and the traffic is thinner on weekday mornings. Be careful in the rain, when the road gets slick and the mist reduces visibility to a few metres.

You will find everything here: petrol stations, banks, pharmacies, cafés and restaurants offering Malay, Chinese, Indian and Western food. Steamboat, a hot pot of broth and vegetables, is a local favourite on a cold night, and the roti canai is excellent in the morning. Book accommodation ahead on weekends and school holidays, when the town fills. A jacket, rain gear and patience are your best equipment.
t.brinchang@4.5,101.4:
Brinchang is a small town on a ridge at about 1,400 metres, and it is the cool, damp heart of the Cameron Highlands. Developed by the British in the 1920s as a hill station after William Cameron mapped the plateau in 1885, the area is known for tea, strawberries and vegetables, which grow on terraces that cover the hills in intense green. Mist hangs over the slopes, and the temperature is far lower than on the lowlands, often below twenty degrees, so a light jacket is welcome. The nearby settlement of Tanah Rata, about three kilometres away, has a larger shopping street, and the nearest city is Ipoh, over thirty kilometres away.

The ride up from the lowlands is the high point of the trip. The road climbs from Tapah through rainforest with a steady series of bends, and the air cools gradually. The surface is variable, with some bumpy sections and areas affected by landslides in the rainy season, and trucks, buses and cars share the road. Fog can come in quickly in the afternoon, so take care, and use your lights. Early morning is best, when the road is quiet and the sunlight comes through the trees.

Tea is the signature. The Boh plantation, founded in the 1920s, has a visitor centre with views over the rows of tea bushes, and you can have a cup of tea and a slice of cake. The Mossy Forest, high above Brinchang at Gunung Brinchang, is a cloud forest where trees are covered with moss and ferns, and the ground is spongy. Strawberry farms sell fruit and ice cream, and the Sungai Palas tea estate is a lovely place to walk. Most of the produce is also sold at local markets, where flowers are plentiful.

Brinchang has fuel stations, restaurants and shops, and also a night market on weekends. Steamboat, a hot pot meal, suits the cool evenings, and scones with jam are a nod to the colonial history. Weekends and school holidays bring heavy traffic, so aim for weekdays. The dry season, around February to April, is most reliable, but showers are possible all year. Enjoy the cool air.
t.kuala kangsar@4.8,100.9:
Kuala Kangsar is the royal town of Perak, the seat of the sultan, and it carries its status lightly. The town sits on the Perak river, Malaysia's second longest, and about forty thousand people live here. The Ubudiah Mosque, with its golden onion dome and white minarets, is among the most beautiful in the country, built in the early twentieth century after the sultan vowed to build one if an elephant that was unable to walk recovered. The Istana Iskandariah, the palace, stands on a hill, and the Perak Royal Museum is housed in a wooden palace built without nails. It is a quiet, dignified place with tree-lined avenues.

Kuala Kangsar has a surprising place in the history of rubber. In 1877, the first rubber seedlings in Malaya were planted here, brought from Kew Gardens, and a descendant of the original trees still stands in the town. Rubber became the engine of the Malayan economy, and the plantations around still shape the landscape. The Malay College, a school modelled on English public schools, trained generations of the elite. The area is also known for a type of pottery, labu sayong, a gourd-shaped water jar.

For a rider, this is the start of the East-West Highway, which runs across the peninsula to the east coast. The road climbs steadily through rainforest, passing the Temenggor Lake and the Belum-Temengor forest complex, which is one of the oldest rainforests in the world. The highway is well surfaced, with long, gentle bends and a few tight sections, but trucks are slow on the grades and wildlife, including elephants, can appear. Mist and rain are common, and the road is quiet at night, so stay alert.

Fill the tank in Kuala Kangsar or Taiping, since the highway has long stretches with few stations. Local food is typical of the north: laksa Kuala Kangsar, a rice-noodle dish with fish gravy, is a local favourite, and the roadside stalls serve strong coffee. The best time to ride is the dry season, though rain can fall anytime. Take a rest in the town, and walk along the river at dusk before heading for the hills.
t.shilin karst naigu stone forest@24.9,103:
Out of the red earth of eastern Yunnan, about eighty kilometres south-east of Kunming, rise the grey stone pinnacles of the Shilin, the Stone Forest, a landscape of limestone that looks like a petrified woodland. The rock was laid down as sediment in a shallow sea around two hundred and seventy million years ago, and then raised, split and carved by rain into towers up to thirty metres high, with sharp ridges and narrow alleys in between. The Naigu area is the older, blacker part, where the stone has been darkened by lichens and weathering, and it is quieter than the main tourist area. The Shilin karst is part of the South China Karst, which UNESCO listed in 2007.

The Stone Forest is also the homeland of the Sani, a branch of the Yi people, who are known for their colourful embroidered costumes, their songs and a legend of a girl named Ashima. According to the story, Ashima was a beautiful and clever girl who was kidnapped by a rich man's son, and she was rescued by her lover, but a flood separated them, and she was turned into a stone pillar in the forest, still waiting. The Sani also celebrate the Torch Festival in summer, a night of bonfires, wrestling and dancing.

Visiting requires some stamina: the paths wind between the stones, up steps and through narrow gaps, and the main parts can be very crowded. Naigu is calmer and has a boardwalk and shaded paths, and the best light is in the early morning or late afternoon, when the stone glows. Yunnan's climate is gentle, with spring-like weather much of the year at about 1,800 metres, though rain falls in summer.

An honest note about riding: bringing a foreign motorbike into China requires special permits, local registration and, in practice, a guide, so most visitors reach Shilin by bus or car from Kunming on the expressway. The roads are excellent and fuel is easy to find in Shilin, a town of about fifty-five thousand people. The local specialities include rice noodles served in a hot broth, grilled goat cheese, and wild mushrooms, which are famous in Yunnan, along with tea and pu'er cakes. Stay for a Sani song performance in the evening if you can, as it gives the stones a human voice.
t.ensemble mixte de hiva oa tahuata@-9.8,-:
Hiva Oa is the second largest of the Marquesas, a long ridge of green peaks leaning into the Pacific, and Tahuata lies a few kilometres off its southern coast like a smaller shadow. The main settlement is Atuona, on a deep bay beneath the mountains, and it is known to the world for two famous graves. Paul Gauguin came here in 1901, tired of Tahiti and the colonial authorities, and died in 1903 in his house he called the House of Pleasure. Jacques Brel, the Belgian singer, arrived in the 1970s, flew his little plane between the islands, and died in 1978. Both lie in the same hillside cemetery at Calvary, looking over the bay, and it is a more moving place than the cheerful frangipani suggests.

The Marquesas themselves have a deeper story. The stone paepae platforms and enormous carved tiki hidden in the valleys, such as the great figures at Puamau on the north-east coast, date back to a large Polynesian society that was ravaged by disease after European contact. The islands are being put forward for recognition as a mixed cultural and natural heritage site, hence this entry.

The riding on Hiva Oa is the real prize. The road from Atuona toward Puamau climbs up a ridge in tight bends and hairpins, drops through palm and breadfruit forest, and crosses a pass with views of rain-lashed valleys. Parts of it are concrete strips or paved, other parts are gravel or mud, and a day with a heavy shower can quickly change the road. It is a fine place for a trail bike, though few visitors bring one, so check with a local pension about hiring. Dry mornings give the best views, and the clouds cap the peaks by afternoon.

Atuona, with about eighteen hundred people, has a couple of shops, a small supermarket, a bank, and a fuel station, so fill up before heading into the interior, since nothing is sold beyond. Local food includes grilled fish, poisson cru, breadfruit and roast pork, and the people are friendly, with strong traditions of carving and tattoo. Respect the tapu around ancient sites, ask before entering, and carry insect repellent against the sand flies, which can bite fiercely.
t.genting sempah@3.3,101.8:
Genting Sempah is the doorway between the lowlands of Selangor and the cool, cloud-wrapped highlands of Pahang, and for riders leaving Kuala Lumpur it is the first sign that the road is about to get interesting. The pass sits on the state border, where the Karak Expressway rises in a long grade through dense rainforest, and a tunnel carries traffic through the ridge. A busy rest area on the old road serves petrol, snacks, roadside stalls and clean toilets, and it is popular with weekend riders who gather to compare machines and plans.

Above the pass rises Genting Highlands, a mountaintop resort at around 1,800 metres, reached by a winding road and by the Awana Skyway, one of the longest cable-car rides in Southeast Asia. The air up there is cool, often shrouded in mist, and a stark contrast to the heat of Kuala Lumpur. On the other side, the town of Bentong is known for its ginger and for durian in the fruiting season, usually June to August, when roadside stalls pile up the spiky fruit. Nearby Bukit Tinggi has a French-themed resort village, an odd surprise among the hills.

The riding is a mix of fast expressway and twisting hill roads. The old Karak road and the climb to Genting have broad, smooth bends and gentle gradients, while the road up to Fraser's Hill, an old hill station started by the British in the early twentieth century, is narrow, steep and one-way in places, with timed traffic. Rain is common, often in sudden, heavy downpours in the afternoon, and the road surface turns slick. Fog can reduce visibility on the heights, so ride with lights on and keep a good distance.

Fuel is easy to find on the expressway rest areas and in Bentong, and the stalls serve nasi lemak, satay and strong, sweet tea. Mornings are the best time, with cooler air and clear views. Bring a rain suit, since a shower is almost guaranteed.
t.bentong food@3.5,101.9:
Bentong is the last proper town before the mountains close in on the road to the east coast, and riders from Kuala Lumpur tend to meet it as a reward after a morning of Genting Highlands switchbacks or the long grind up the Karak Highway. It sits in Pahang, in a bowl of low green hills, with a river running through and a population of roughly fifty thousand. The town has the unhurried feel of a place that was built for tin and rubber and now lives on trade, farming and passing traffic.

What Bentong is known for is ginger. Ginger from this district has a reputation across Malaysia for being fiery and fragrant, and you will see it in the market, in tea, in sweets and in dishes in the coffee shops. The coffee shops themselves are the real attraction. Order a kopi and something from a hawker stall, sit under a ceiling fan with the town drifting by, and you have the full Bentong experience. Chinese Malaysian cooking dominates the old centre, with noodles, steamed buns and pork or chicken rice, and there are Malay and Indian options all within a short walk.

The riding to get here is a mix. From Kuala Lumpur the road climbs through jungle on the old Genting corridor, with curves among tall trees, moist air and sudden changes in temperature. Rain is usually part of the deal, and heavy afternoon downpours are common, so plan to be dry and fed by early afternoon. The road surface is generally decent, but watch for oil, wet leaves and sudden trucks around bends. Monkeys occasionally sit on the verge and are best ignored.

Fuel is straightforward. A town of this size has several stations on the main road, and it is a sensible place to fill up before heading toward Raub or Fraser's Hill. Rest rooms and parking are easy near the market area. There is also a bit of history if you want it, because the Raub area to the north was once Malaya's major gold-mining district, and old mining sites and heritage buildings still tell the story.

Stay hydrated, wear ventilated gear, and leave time for a second coffee. In this climate, it is not an indulgence but a form of risk management.
t.fraser s hill road@3.7,101.7:
Fraser's Hill is a small hill station about twelve hundred metres up in the Titiwangsa range, and the road to it is the best argument for owning a motorcycle in Malaysia. The settlement was made a retreat in the British colonial era, and its name comes from Louis James Fraser, a trader said to have run mule trains and a mining business here before he vanished around the early twentieth century. Today it is a sleepy place of mock-Tudor cottages, a clock tower, a small golf course and a quiet sense of leftover Englishness, with mist drifting through the pines.

The notorious part is the final climb. The old road from the Gap, a pass where the highway splits, is narrow and runs one way at a time. Traffic is allowed up and down in alternating periods, controlled by timing, so you need to check the schedule at the Gap before committing. That makes the approach feel like a ceremony. When it is your turn, the road squeezes through dense jungle with tight bends, steep walls of green and the cool air thickening with each hairpin.

The rewards are clear. The air is noticeably cooler up here, and the forest is full of birds. Fraser's Hill is among the best birdwatching sites in Peninsular Malaysia, and early mornings bring the sound of calls across the valley. Even if birds are not your thing, the scenery is a refreshing change from the humid lowlands. Wet-weather riding is the norm, so be prepared for slick surfaces, fog and leaf litter on the tarmac.

Raub, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest sizable town, and you should arrive with fuel in the tank. Do not rely on finding services up the hill at the hours you need them. Kuala Kubu Bharu and Bentong are good places to top up before the climb.

Take a rain layer even if the morning looks bright. The weather turns fast in the hills, and the temperature can drop enough that a thin jacket feels welcome. Go early, ride carefully, and give yourself time to be slow. The road is the point, and the slower you take it, the more of it you see.
t.kuala kubu bharu@3.6,101.7:
Kuala Kubu Bharu is where riders leaving Kuala Lumpur northward get their last sure supply of fuel before the road to Fraser's Hill, and it is a better stop than the name of a fuel waypoint suggests. The name means New Kuala Kubu, which hints at a story. The old town was a tin-mining settlement that suffered severe flooding, and the authorities laid out a new town on higher ground in the early twentieth century, with the neat planned layout, shophouse rows and tree-lined streets that still give it a faintly colonial calm.

It sits in the valley of the Selangor River, where the western foothills of the Titiwangsa range begin to rise. On a clear morning the hills show blue behind the rooftops, and the jungle pushes close to the edge of the settlement. The town is small enough to walk end to end, and the market area has the usual good kopitiam and stalls. The old part is quiet even at midday, and there is a rhythm of ordinary life you do not see on the expressway.

For the ride, the point of Kuala Kubu Bharu is the gateway behaviour. South of here you have the busy industrial belt around Rawang and Serendah, with trucks and traffic lights. North of here the road narrows, the traffic thins and the jungle gets thicker. The route toward Fraser's Hill leads through the district's villages and rubber plantations before reaching the Gap and the single-lane climb. Roadside fruit stalls appear in the season, with durian, rambutan and mangosteen on offer if you are lucky with the months.

Practicalities are simple. Rest stops are easy, with shaded seating around the market and a few simple eateries. In the heat, drink more water than you think you need, because ventilated jackets hide how much you are sweating.

Go early. Weekends bring day-trippers from the city, and by mid-morning the road toward the hills has more cars than corners. Leave before eight and you have the best of it.
t.aire marine cotiere de ua huka@-8.9,-139:
Ua Huka is the dry, rugged island of the Marquesas, where the wind blows steadily, the hills are bare and brown, and herds of wild horses graze on the plateau. The island has about six hundred people, living in three villages, Vaipaee, Hane and Hokatu, and its coastline is lined with cliffs, sea caves, and small offshore islets that are important nesting sites for seabirds. The marine area around it is a protected stretch of water, rich in fish, rays and sometimes dolphins.

Riding on Ua Huka is about as modest and as memorable as it gets. A few narrow roads, some concrete and some rough, link the villages and climb across the island's central ridge, and the views over the surf-whipped coast are splendid. Do not expect a big circuit. You are travelling on a very small island with very few vehicles, plenty of wandering horses, goats and chickens, and sudden steep bends. Weather is mostly dry and breezy, with the island lying in the rain shadow of its higher neighbours, though squalls can blow in off the ocean. Getting here normally means a boat from Nuku Hiva, or a small plane, so plan around their timetables.

The island is known for craftsmanship, particularly wood carving and stone sculpture, and the museum in Vaipaee has displays of Marquesan artefacts, tools and carvings, a good place to see how important the arts were to this culture. The islanders carve rosewood and miki miki wood into bowls, tikis and ornaments. Archaeologists have also found petroglyphs and old ceremonial sites in the valleys. Down at the shoreline, birds nest in thousands on the offshore rocks, and the sound of surf in the sea caves is deep and constant.

Practical matters are as simple as the island. A couple of small shops and family guesthouses provide meals, often built on fresh fish, goat, breadfruit and fruit, and fuel is available in very limited amounts for local vehicles, so do not count on it for touring. Carry cash in Pacific francs, a hat and sunscreen, and plenty of water, since the sun on the dry plateau can be harsh. Ask before photographing people and sacred places, and bring a spirit of patience. On Ua Huka the day runs at the speed of the horses.
t.sapa@22.3,103.8:
Sa Pa sits at about 1,500 meters in the Hoang Lien Son mountains of northwest Vietnam, and the mist that drifts in over its terraced valleys is half of its character. The French established a hill station here in the early twentieth century, building villas where colonial officials could escape the heat of the lowlands, and some of those stone buildings survive. Today it is a bustling market town for the Hmong, Red Dao, Tay and other mountain peoples, whose embroidered clothing, indigo-dyed cloth and silver jewelry make the Saturday market one of the most colorful in the country.

The landscape surrounds you. Fansipan, at 3,143 meters, is the highest mountain in Indochina and rises just south-west of the town, and a cable car opened in 2016 takes visitors most of the way up in minutes. Below, the Muong Hoa valley is cut into rice terraces that follow every contour, green in summer, golden in early autumn, and mirror-like in the planting season. Villages such as Lao Chai and Ta Van lie along the valley floor, and the paths between them are popular for walking.

For riders, this is mountain country in the full sense. The road from Lao Cai climbs steeply on Highway 4D with tight bends, fog and heavy trucks and buses, so it demands attention. Beyond Sa Pa the road continues over Tram Ton Pass, often called O Quy Ho, at around two thousand meters the highest road pass in Vietnam. The weather changes sharply from one side to the other, with cool cloud on the Sa Pa side and warm sun on the Lai Chau side. The surface can be wet and slippery, with occasional landslides in the rainy season from May to September, so check conditions locally.

The best seasons are autumn, from about September to November, when the rice is ripe and the air clearer, and spring, when the hills are fresh. Winter is cold and can bring frost or even a little snow.

Services are good for a town of its size. Sa Pa has a handful of petrol stations on the main road, plenty of small hotels and restaurants, and a number of cafes with views across the valley. Try the grilled skewers sold in the evening, and the hot rice wine that locals drink with them. Rain gear is essential at any time of year.
t.cultural landscape of honghe hani rice t:
In the southern Yunnan prefecture of Honghe, on the slopes of the Ailao Mountains above the Red River, the Hani people have spent more than a thousand years carving rice paddies into the hillsides. The terraces climb from the valley floor at a few hundred meters to over a thousand, in layers so fine that from above they look like contour lines drawn on the land. UNESCO inscribed the Honghe Hani Rice Terraces as a Cultural Landscape in 2013, recognizing not just the beauty of the fields but the system that feeds them.

That system is a lesson in how to live on a steep slope. Forest on the mountaintop captures moisture and feeds streams, which flow down through the Hani villages, with their mushroom-shaped thatched roofs, and then through channels into the paddies below. Water is shared according to traditional rules, and the fields are stocked with fish and ducks as well as rice. It is a closed, careful cycle, and it has lasted because everyone in the community depends on it.

The best time to visit is from late November to March, when the paddies are flooded and reflect the sky in hundreds of mirrors, with the morning mist drifting through. Viewpoints around Yuanyang, such as Duoyishu, Bada and Laohuzui, are popular at sunrise and sunset, when the light turns the water pink and gold. In summer the fields are green, but the cloud and rain make visibility poor. The town of Xinjie, in Yuanyang County, has guesthouses and simple restaurants.

For riders, the road is the old story of southern Yunnan: long climbs on narrow mountain roads, with tight hairpins, local trucks and the occasional herd of buffalo. The surface varies, with newer sections smooth and older ones broken by landslides and rain. Fog often drops without warning in winter, which is the best photography season but also the most hazardous for driving. Foreign visitors cannot ride their own motorcycles in China without a Chinese permit and registration, so independent riding needs local arrangements.

Services in the area are basic outside the main towns, and fuel is better found in Yuanyang or in Mengzi, the nearest city of any size. Bring layers, since the altitude and humidity make it colder than it looks.

The old road into the Cameron Highlands from Tapah is a ride that regulars talk about with a mixture of affection and dread. It climbs from the hot lowlands of Perak into the cool mountains through endless bends, tight and blind, cut into steep jungle slopes, with waterfalls tumbling down beside the road and the trees closing in overhead. It is narrow, it is often wet, and it is used by buses and lorries that take their half of the road out of the middle. It is also one of the most memorable climbs in Malaysia.

South of Tanah Rata, the road passes Ringlet, a small town that is the first sign that you have arrived in the highlands, with a reservoir created for a hydroelectric scheme and the first tea estates on the hills around. The tea plantations are the defining landscape of the Cameron Highlands: rows of bright green bushes covering whole hillsides like corduroy, with workers picking leaves by hand or with shears, and factories where the leaves are dried and processed. Some estates have visitor centres and tea rooms with views over the valleys.

The highlands were named after a British surveyor who mapped the area in the 1880s, and they were developed as a hill station in the 1920s and 1930s, a place where colonial officials could escape the heat. Tea, vegetables and flowers followed, and the area still supplies much of Malaysia's fresh produce. It was here, too, that an American silk businessman famously disappeared on a walk in the jungle in 1967, a mystery that has never been solved and that still fuels speculation.

The climate is cool and damp, with temperatures that rarely rise above the mid-twenties and fall well below that at night. Rain is common, especially in the afternoon, and fog can roll in quickly. The roads are busy at weekends and holidays, when people from Kuala Lumpur and Ipoh come up to escape the heat, so ride it midweek if you possibly can. Tanah Rata, a few kilometres away, has fuel, hotels, restaurants and shops, and it is the main town of the highlands. Try the local tea with scones, a colonial habit that has become a local tradition.

North of Tanah Rata, the Cameron Highlands get higher, busier and more intensely farmed. The road climbs through Brinchang, the second town of the highlands, known for its night market and strawberry stalls, and then on towards Kea Farm and Tringkap, where the hillsides are covered not with tea but with plastic greenhouses growing vegetables, flowers and strawberries. It is not the prettiest part of the highlands, but it is the engine room, supplying much of the produce sold in Malaysia and Singapore.

Above Brinchang, a narrow road leads to the summit of Gunung Brinchang, at just over two thousand metres the highest point in Peninsular Malaysia reachable by road. Near the top is the Mossy Forest, a cloud forest where the trees are twisted, stunted and covered in thick layers of moss, ferns and orchids, and where the air is permanently damp. A boardwalk lets you walk through it, and on a clear day the views across the forested mountains are spectacular, though clear days are rare. The road to the top passes through tea estates, including one of the largest in the highlands, with a cafe overlooking the plantations.

The highlands have a complicated history. The area was originally home to Orang Asli groups, the indigenous peoples of Peninsular Malaysia, who still live in villages in the forests around. Chinese, Indian and Malay communities came later, working in the tea estates and farms, and the mix of cultures shows in the temples, food and markets of the towns. Development has been rapid and sometimes uncontrolled, with forest cleared for farms, and landslides and floods have become a problem.

The riding here is slower and more congested than the climb from Tapah, with traffic jams in Brinchang at weekends and narrow, steep side roads up to the farms. The road north towards Simpang Pulai and Ipoh is a newer, wider route that descends in long curves to the lowlands, offering a different kind of ride. Fuel, food and accommodation are plentiful in Brinchang and Tanah Rata. The weather is cool, and in the evening it can be chilly, so bring a warm layer.
